newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's Cools murder exposed web of corruption.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's Cools murder exposed web of corruption.

text.p: Five years ago five shots rang out in the early morning in the car park of a block of flats near the southeastern Belgian town of Liege, as a professional killer gunned down a prominent politician.

The echoes of those shots still reverberate, after investigators into the murder of francophone socialist Andre Cools uncovered a trail of intrigue, theft and bribery reaching to the heart of government.
On Friday police in Liege finally arrested four people in connection with the killing.

Fallout from the murder on on July 18, 1991, has forced a handful of senior socialist politicians from both the French and the Dutch sides of the country's linguistic divide to resign, and an airforce general to kill himself.
The heads of two major Italian and French firms have been called for questioning.

Most prominent victim of the scandals that have rocked the government since the killing was NATO Secretary General Willy Claes -- forced to resign last October after being implicated in a political slush fund scandal uncovered by the Cools investigators.

That scandal, involving more than 100 million Belgian francs ($3 million) paid into secret Socialist Party accounts by Italian helicopter firm Agusta and French aviation giant Dassault in return for lucrative contracts, happened when Claes was Belgium's Economic Affairs Minister.
Claes has repeatedly denied any knowledge of the slush fund.

But it has proved to be the most significant path uncovered by the team of murder investigators, costing not only Claes his job but also Foreign Minister and former Flemish Socialist Party President Frank Vandenbroucke who resigned in March last year.
Three francophone Socialist Party politicians, Guy Coeme, Guy Mathot and Guy Spitaels were also forced to resign although they were all re-elected by loyal voters in elections last year.
Air force General Jacques Lefebvre committed suicide in a Brussels hotel room in March last year over the Dassault affair.
Magistrates investigating the tangled Cools case have issued an international arrest warrant against Dassault chief Serge Dassault, who in turn denies all knowledge of the alleged bribes.
While the political slush fund trail could yet produce fresh victims, it has not shed any more light on the motive for the murder.

Like the other lines of inquiry covering stolen shares, a mysterious fire on the night before the murder in the car of Cools' chief of staff Lambert Verjus and alleged embezzlement by former senior staff at insurance firm SMAP, it has thrown up all sorts of clues but no hard reasons.
The Cools affair -- like Italy's anti-corruption Operation Clean Hands -- has shaken Belgian politics to the core.
"It has all proved that no-one is untouchable anymore," a senior Belgian legal source said.
